vt20_yeshua_record_r.topic: The historical Yeshua: non-Christian notices, dates, name, kingdom sayings, Mark's date, the image of Jesus

claims.text: Josephus, Antiquities XX.9.1 (c.93-94 CE): the high priest Ananus brought before the Sanhedrin 'the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James' and had him stoned; citizens appealed to Agrippa and Albinus and Ananus was removed after three months

Most scholars hold the Testimonium Flavianum (Ant. 18.63-64) partly authentic with Christian additions ('if it be lawful to call him a man', 'He was the Christ', the resurrection report); the James passage's authenticity 'almost universally acknowledged' (Feldman); Ken Olson's whole-forgery-by-Eusebius thesis a minority view (Feldman adopted it 2012; Carleton Paget and Whealey rejected it); Pines 1971 published Agapius' 10th-c. Arabic version ('Pilate condemned him to be crucified')

Tacitus, Annals XV.44: Nero blamed the fire of Rome on 'Christians'; 'Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus'

Yeshua was a common shortened form of Yehoshua (Joshua) in the Second Temple period; on 71 burial finds (Kloner: 'one of the common names'); Tal Ilan counts 85 Yeshua; Greek Iesous; meaning roughly 'YHWH saves'

Most scholars place Jesus' birth c.6-4 BCE (before Herod's death, 4 BCE per Schürer); crucifixion between 30 and 36 CE, Pilate prefect from 26 to 36/37; astronomical candidates 7 April 30 and 3 April 33

Luke 17:21 entos hymon: RSV/NRSV and many modern versions 'among/in the midst of you'; KJV, Luther, Vulgate (intra vos), Peshitta 'within/inside'; Ramelli (2009) argues 'inside' is correct, 'among' 'practically unattested' in Greek, patristic readers (Origen, Athanasius) read 'inside'; cites Thomas 3 and 113 as parallels
Gospel of Thomas saying 3 (Lambdin): 'the kingdom is inside of you, and it is outside of you'; saying 113: 'the kingdom of the father is spread out upon the earth, and men do not see it'

Thomas survives in three Greek Oxyrhynchus fragments (P.Oxy 1 shortly after 200; 654; 655 mid-3rd c.) and one Coptic copy (shortly before 350); composition estimates 50-140 CE, Patterson 70-80, Cameron late 1st c.; first clear attestation Hippolytus 222-235
Mark 1:15: 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel'
Mark is dated around 70 CE (Mark 13 and the Temple's destruction), most scholars think it the earliest gospel, and it is anonymous

Joan Taylor, What Did Jesus Look Like? (2018): olive-brown skin, brown-black hair, brown eyes, about 165 cm, probably short hair; earliest images show a philosopher type; the long-haired bearded type from the 4th-7th c. borrowed from Serapis/Zeus

Blum and Harvey, The Color of Christ (2012): Gospels never describe Jesus' looks; white Jesus widespread in the US in the early 1800s; 1880s-1910s more blond/blue-eyed under immigration fears; William Apess 1830s called Jesus 'a man of color'; Sallman's Head of Christ among the most reproduced images
Warner Sallman's Head of Christ (1940) reproduced more than 500 million times by the end of the 20th century
Nostra Aetate 4 (28 October 1965): what happened in Christ's passion 'cannot be charged against all the Jews, without distinction, then alive, nor against the Jews of today'
Luke 17:20-21: asked by the Pharisees when the kingdom of God would come, he answered that it is not coming 'in ways that can be observed'; ESV renders entos hymon 'in the midst of you'
The Great Fire of Rome began on the night of 18-19 July 64 CE under Nero; Tacitus, Annals XV.44, is the source for Nero's blaming it on the Christians

vt20_paul_r.topic: Paul: letters, revelation claim, meetings with Cephas and James, Jerusalem meeting and Antioch dispute

claims.text: Gal 1:11-12: Paul's gospel 'is not of human origin'; 'I received it through a revelation of Jesus Christ'; 1:16-17 he 'did not confer with any human being', went to Arabia and back to Damascus
Gal 1:18-19: after three years he went to Jerusalem to visit Cephas for fifteen days and saw no other apostle except 'James the Lord's brother'

Gal 2:1-10: fourteen years later, with Barnabas and Titus; Titus not compelled to be circumcised; James, Cephas and John, 'acknowledged pillars', gave 'the right hand of fellowship', dividing the mission; asked only that they 'remember the poor'; 2:6 the leaders 'contributed nothing to me'

Gal 2:11-14: at Antioch Paul opposed Cephas to his face after Cephas stopped eating with Gentiles when 'certain people came from James'; 2:16 justified 'not by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ'
1 Cor 15:3: 'I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received'; 15:5-8 appearances to Cephas, the Twelve, more than 500, James, all the apostles, and last to Paul
1 Cor 11:23: 'I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you' (the Last Supper words); 1 Cor 7:10 '(not I, but the Lord)' on divorce versus 7:12 '(I, not the Lord)'

Paul born c.5 BCE-5 CE in Tarsus, a Pharisee, persecuted the early believers; conversion c.31-36; 'did not know Jesus during his lifetime' but knew Peter and James; traditionally martyred in Rome under Nero between 64 and 68, with no New Testament account of his death

Seven undisputed letters: Romans, 1-2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon; Ephesians and the Pastorals considered pseudepigraphical by most critical scholars; Colossians and 2 Thessalonians divided; Hebrews anonymous; 13 letters bear Paul's name

The Jerusalem meeting is generally dated c.48-50; most scholars identify Acts 15 with Gal 2:1-10; the Acts 'apostolic decree' asks Gentiles to abstain from idol food, blood, strangled meat and porneia
1 Tim 3:1: 'If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task'; 3:2 lists the overseer's qualifications
Phil 3:5: Paul describes himself as 'a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee'
The Great Fire of Rome began on the night of 18-19 July 64 CE

vt20_communities_r.topic: First communities: house churches, common purse, Paul's collection, Didache, Justin, Pliny, Ignatius, no tithe

claims.text: Acts 2:44-46: believers 'had all things in common', sold possessions and distributed 'as any had need', attended the temple daily and broke bread 'in their homes'
Acts 4:32-35: 'of one heart and soul', 'everything in common', 'not a needy person among them', distributed to each 'as any had need'; Barnabas, a Levite of Cyprus, sold a field
Acts 5:1-4: Ananias and Sapphira kept back part of the price; Peter: 'While it remained unsold, did it not remain your own?' — the fault charged is lying, not keeping property
Acts usually dated 80-90 CE (some 110-120), by the author of Luke; most scholars treat it as historiography with theological aims
1 Cor 16:1-4: collection for the saints, as directed to Galatia; 'On the first day of every week' each to put something aside 'as he may prosper'; carried to Jerusalem by people the church accredits
2 Cor 9:5-7: 'a willing gift, not as an exaction'; 'not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver'
Rom 16:1-7: Phoebe 'a servant [or deaconess] of the church at Cenchreae'; Prisca and Aquila and 'the church in their house'; Andronicus and Junia 'well known to the apostles'

Didache 11: an apostle stays one day, two if needed; 'if he ask money, he is a false prophet'; 13: true prophet worthy of support, first-fruits to the prophets 'for they are your high priests', if none give to the poor; money and clothing 'as it may seem good to you'; 14: gather every Lord's day and break bread; 15: 'appoint for yourselves bishops and deacons worthy of the Lord'
Didache dated 50-120, 'new consensus' c.100 (Draper); published by Bryennios 1883 from Codex Hierosolymitanus 54 copied 1056

Justin, First Apology 67 (c.155): gathering on 'the day called Sunday', memoirs of the apostles read, the 'president' teaches; 'they who are well to do, and willing, give what each thinks fit'; deposited with the president for orphans, widows, sick, prisoners, strangers
Irenaeus AH IV.18.2 (c.180): the Jews had 'the tithes of their goods consecrated to Him'; Christians 'set aside all their possessions for the Lord's purposes'

Catholic Encyclopedia: clergy support 'in the beginning' came from 'the spontaneous offerings of the faithful'; earliest positive church legislation on tithes the bishops' letter at Tours 567 and the Council of Mâcon 585; earliest civil enforcement Charlemagne's capitularies late 8th c.

Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 8: 'See that you all follow the bishop'; 'Wherever the bishop shall appear, there let the multitude also be'; 'not lawful without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate a love-feast'
Ignatius traditionally died c.108 under Trajan; dates debated (110s or c.150; Barnes 140s); earliest writer to stress a single bishop with presbyters and deacons; first known use of 'catholic church'

Pliny, Ep. 10.96 (governor of Bithynia-Pontus c.111): Christians met on a fixed day before dawn, sang to Christ 'as to a god', swore not to commit fraud, theft, adultery, shared 'ordinary and innocent food'; two female slaves called deaconesses tortured; Trajan 10.97 forbade seeking Christians out or anonymous accusations
Dura-Europos: house built 232/233, converted to a church probably 240/241, abandoned 256; a private house converted for Christian use; Good Shepherd as a young beardless man
Ignatius was bishop of Antioch (successor of Evodius per Eusebius); while en route to Rome, where he was to be killed, he wrote a series of letters (six to churches, one to Polycarp)
Justin's First Apology is dated between 155 and 157 CE, from its reference to Lucius Munatius Felix as a recent prefect of Egypt
